newsitem.title: POLAND: Thousands protest over Polish student's murder.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest over Polish student's murder.

text.p: Thousands of appalled Poles marched silently in pouring rain through Warsaw on Monday to protest over the torture-murder of a young student by hooligans and to demand better protection by the law.

The march was a horrified reaction to the killing of secondary school graduate Tomasz Jaworski, 19, who was abducted, tortured over two days and then knifed to death -- apparently because he and friends held a picnic at a spot that a local youth gang viewed as its territory.

"Tomek is dead, brutally murdered for no reason," read a banner held by a procession of some 4,000 people that carried lighted candles to the suburban Warsaw woods where Jaworski was grabbed on June 13 by the armed gang as he and friends celebrated passing their final examinations.
The sombre march, held in quiet broken only by prayers intoned by a priest is the latest in a series over the last two years showing that Poles are deeply alarmed by violent crime.

A similar event in Warsaw last year, over the death of a student shot on the street by a fleeing robber, attracted more than 10,000 participants and was the largest protest in the capital for several years.
This time police estimated the crowd at 4,000, including fellow pupils of the dead man, old people and children.
In an anguished letter to Jaworski's schoolmates published on Monday, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said of such crimes: "I view these incidents as a national tragedy,"
He said law enforcement had to be made more effective but distanced himself from arguments that harsher penalties were the solution and argued for addressing social origins of crime.

"We must radically increase the effectiveness and efficiency of the police and the justice system, while remembering that even the harshest penalty will not eliminate aggression, hatred and unreasoning bestiality," he wrote.
But many of the marchers were calling for the penal code, just reformed by parliament in a bill which finally abolished the long-suspended death penalty, to be made harsher.
"We must tighten the penal code, have more severe penalites and make the police more effective," said a classmate of the dead man holding a banner on the march.
"We want to touch the conscience of those who decide on what goes on in our country and on the state of our law," said the student, who would only give his first name, also Tomasz.
"None of my three sons knows how to fight and they never will, so any bandit who feels like it can do them harm," said Antonina Kowalska, 42, with her two-year-old boy on the march.
Police say they have detained four people suspected of involvement in Jaworski's death, including a 24-year-old mother of three.
They are still hunting for others among the gang who beat the students at the picnic site and abducted Jaworski, possibly because he may have recognised the attackers.
Crime rates in Poland are still below those of most Western European countries and the former Soviet states but they have risen steeply since the 1989 fall of communism.
